note:
Paul describes himself as “apostle,” but not his associate (also 1 Cor.1:1; Col. 1:1). A man who held the office of apostle was an eyewitness of the resurrection (Acts 1:22; 1 Cor. 15:8) who had been personally appointed by Christ (“of Jesus Christ,” see Matt. 10:1–7; Acts 1:24–26; Gal. 1:1) to govern the early church (1 Thess. 4:8; 2 Thess. 3:6, 14), and to teach or write with authority (1 Cor. 14:37; 1 Thess. 2:13; 4:15; 2 Pet. 3:15, 16) as one who had received special revelation from God (Eph. 2:20; 3:5). The term is used as a title of the twelve disciples and Paul in a distinctive sense. It is also used in a broader sense (Rom. 16:7), while in general or nontechnical use it means a “messenger” or “representative” (8:23; Phil. 2:25). When used in this way, it does not refer to a specific ordained office.

**by the will of God.** It is God’s sovereign choice that ultimately places people in church offices and ministries. The apostolic office was extraordinary and temporary, and it passed away once the last surviving eyewitness of the resurrection died and the NT was completed. The ordinary church offices continue to be necessary and are filled by elders (Acts 20:28) and others whose gifts equip them for ministries (1 Cor. 12:7, 11, 28). An individual’s calling to one of the ordinary church offices is confirmed by the people of God as the church discerns who has the gifts and qualifications for the work (Eph. 4:11). Two ordinary church offices, elder and deacon, receive special attention in Scripture (Acts 6:1–6; 1 Tim. 3:1–13; Titus 1:5–9), but other callings are mentioned as well, including evangelist, shepherd (pastor), and teacher. Those callings, enumerated in Ephesians 4:11, are sometimes considered ordinary church offices as well, but it is possible that they are just callings and not ordained offices. Ephesians 4:11 also mentions the office of prophet, but as that was an extraordinary office given to establish the foundation of the church, it likewise passed away once the apostles had laid the church’s foundation in their preaching and teaching (cf.Eph. 2:19–21).

**saints.** Lit. “holy ones.” Paul commonly uses the term to refer to all Christians (Rom. 15:25; Phil. 1:1).

**in the whole of Achaia.** Though the letter was intended primarily for the church at Corinth, Paul apparently realized that it would be read by neighboring churches in the region of Achaia, the southern part of modern Greece. On Corinth, see note on Acts 18:1.

Grace is God’s undeserved favor—not just in initial forgiveness of sins, but in the ordinary events of everyday life as well.

**peace.** The outward blessing of social order and the inward blessing of a good relationship with God (Rom. 5:1; 1 Tim. 2:2).

**God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.** It is evidence of the deity of Christ that He with the Father should be mentioned equally as the origin of grace and peace for the Corinthian church.

verse_quote: Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
note:
The three persons of the Trinity are equally divine, yet they are one God, not three. As the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit suggest, the three persons of the Godhead are distinguished bytheir distinctive personal properties and corresponding relationships to one another. The Father begets the Son and the Son is begotten of the Father from all eternity. Therefore, Paul speaks of the Father in these terms.

**Father of mercies and God of all comfort.** A key theme of chs. 1–9.All consolation and encouragement in the world has its origin in God Himself.

It appears that Paul was criticized by some in Corinth because of his sufferings (see 11:21–30; 12:1–10; 1 Cor.4:6–13). Paul, however, viewed his experience of suffering and God’s comfort to him in affliction as both a confirmation of his apostolic calling and a source of encouragement to other believers.

**that we may be able to comfort.** God has a sovereign purpose both in our troubles and in the comfort that He gives us in them. If we have experienced God’s comfort in suffering, we may be able to support others whose sufferings are like ours.

verse_quote: we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings.
note: Not that we can add anything to Christ’s suffering for us (Is. 53:11; John 19:30; Heb. 9:26–28), but God has called us to suffer for Christ and so to follow in His steps (Rom. 8:17; Col. 1:24; Heb. 12:2, 3; 1 Pet. 2:21). Because believers are united to Christ and are spiritually part of His body, both our sufferings for the gospel and the comfort God provides in Christ are a result of our participation in Him (Phil. 3:10, 11), as the risen Lord had implied when He accused Saul of persecuting Him by persecuting His church (Acts 9:5).Here Paul hints at apersistent feature of his teaching. The key experiences of Christ, especially His suffering, death, and resurrection, are the pattern by which Christians can understand their own suffering and final triumph.
Paul sees God’s sovereign hand and redemptive purpose in everything that happens to him, whether distress or comfort.

Behind this verse lies Paul’s teaching that all believers, as members of one body of Christ, are joined together so that every dimension of life in Christ is shared among them (1 Cor. 12:26). The more fully this reality influences the attitudes and actions of believers toward each other, the more fully they experience satisfying fellowship through Christ with one another.

verse_quote: the affliction we experienced in Asia.
note:
Apparently, he refers to some hardship, persecution, illness, or injurythat he suffered since he last saw his readers. These hardships would have occurred either in Ephesus or between Ephesus and Macedonia, although they are not mentioned in the summary statement of Acts 20:1.

**our.** In this letter, Paul normally uses the editorial plural “we” or “our” to refer to himself alone.

verse_quote: we had received the sentence of death.
note:
Paul was convinced that God had decided it was time for him to die.

**rely not on ourselves.** God’s purpose in our afflictions often is to drive us to this conclusion.

**who raises the dead.** The resurrection of the dead is a revelation of God’s unsurpassable power (Eph. 1:20). It is God’s resurrection power (and not Paul’s own “strength”) that resulted in his past deliverance and will result in his final deliverance from death itself (v.10).

Prayer has real results. God has ordained His relationship to the world in such a way that He will respond to our prayers. Even Paul needed and sought the prayers of others, and he anticipated that God would act on his behalf in answer to the saints’ prayers (Rom. 15:30–32; Eph. 6:19, 20; Phil. 1:19, 20).

**many will give thanks.** These thanks go to God because He delivered Paul from death (v. 10). One of God’s purposes in answering prayer is that we will praise Him for it.

Paul boasts not in his own ability, but in having a clear conscience and morally upright conduct. Paul’s simplicity and godly sincerity are not the result of following the conventional wisdom of the world, but depend on “the grace of God.” When Paul boasts, he takes no credit for himself. It is the triumph of God’s grace in him. Later in this epistle, Paul will match the self-centered boasts of the “super-apostles” with his own “boasts” about his sufferings and his weaknesses (11:30; 12:9, 10).

**earthly wisdom.** In this verse, Paul introduces his denial of the charge that he had worldly motives for changing his plans to visit Corinth. Distinguishing divine wisdom (expressed in the cross of Christ) from “earthly” wisdom was a problem for some Corinthian believers. Worldly wisdom led to divisions in the Corinthian church (1 Cor. 1:10–4:7), and by the standards of such wisdom, Paul was not acceptable as an apostle (10:2–6).

Paul reminds the Corinthians that his writings, like his ministry, are not dishonest or tricky, full of hidden meanings and concealed aims, as perhaps some of his opponents at Corinth had claimed. Paul’s writings were clear enough. In the same way, all Scripture is written not mainly for scholars but for all believers. It is understandable to those who will read it with a willingness to obey it, all the while seeking God’s help in understanding it (Deut. 6:6, 7; Ps. 19:7; 119:130; Matt. 12:3, 5; 19:14; 21:42; Col. 4:16).

verse_quote: the day of our Lord Jesus.
note:
The day of Christ’s return.

**you will boast of us.** They should be proud of what God has done for them in Paul.

Another translation is, “have double grace.” Paul knows that his visits impart God’s grace to churches (cf. Rom. 1:13). His original plan to visit Corinth both on his way to Macedonia in the north and on his return (v. 16) en route to Judea (chs. 8, 9) would have enabled him to minister God’s grace to the Corinthians twice over.

In order to give the Corinthians time to repent in response to a sorrowful letter (not extant) that he had sent with Titus, Paul had revised the earlier plan to visit Corinth before traveling to Macedonia. Consequently, some were charging Paul with changing his plans on a whim rather than following through on his commitments. He needed to explain the pastoral motive—his Christlike commitment to their spiritual welfare—that necessitated the revision of travel plans.

**according to the flesh.** Such plans would be unreliable, vacillating, and unpredictable. Opponents were discrediting the apostle by charging that his change in plans showed weakness of character and lack of integrity. They did not have all the facts, however, and were using these circumstances to attack someone they had already condemned.

Paul calls on God’s faithfulness as the pattern and guarantee for his own faithfulness.

**word.** Paul reminds them that his gospel message was absolutely reliable and led to their salvation.

The absolute truthfulness and reliability of God’s words in Christ are the standard that Paul follows in his own speech. This is consistent with Paul’s general pattern of deriving moral absolutes from the character of God.

Christ fulfills all of God’s promises to His people in the OT, and all our confidence in God’s promises must come from our trust in Jesus Christ as a person whom we know and upon whom we can rely. These OT promises have begun to be fulfilled in Christ’s first coming, and they will be consummated at His last coming.

**we utter our Amen.** “Amen” is derived from a Hb. word expressing agreement with and confidence in what has just been spoken: “so be it” or “it is true” (1 Cor.14:16; Rev.3:14; 22:20).

This Trinitarian passage points to the roles of all three divine persons in salvation.

**1:21 God ...establishes us.** Paul now turns to the ministry of the Holy Spirit to explain how God ensures the perseverance of His people (cf. v. 22). The ability to persevere, that is, to continue in the Christian life, is not from ourselves; it is a gift from God. God gives this ability to all who are born again (Phil. 1:6; 1 Pet. 1:5). Those who are guarded by God in this way continue to trust in Christ throughout their lives (13:5; Col. 1:23; Heb. 3:14), because God protects them through the faith He gives them (v.24).None of them can fall away. If one has been justified, one will most certainly be glorified (Rom. 8:28–30).

**anointed.** To “anoint” literally is to pour oil on the head, often as a sign of divine calling and empowerment (1 Sam. 2:10; 16:13 and notes). The verb “anoint” and the noun “Christ” are derived from the same Gk. root. Every believer is anointed with the Holy Spirit, just as Jesus was anointed with the Holy Spirit (1 John 2:20, 27).

**1:22 put his seal on us.** An official seal indicated authority or ownership and guaranteed protection (Esth. 8:8;Dan.6:17;Matt.27:66;Rev.7:3).God seals us, not with a physical seal of wax, but with the Holy Spirit in our hearts (Eph. 1:13; 4:30). This inward work takes place in a person only once, when he receives and rests on Christ alone for his salvation.

**guarantee.** The Gk. word means a deposit or down payment that is part of the total and that guarantees the whole payment will be made. The Holy Spirit is the guarantee and part of the complete salvation yet to be realized (5:5; Rom. 8:23; Eph. 1:14). Christians already have heavenly life within them, before they reach heaven (1 Cor. 3:16; Col. 1:27). This term is Paul’s third way in vv. 21, 22 of describing the ministry of the Spirit to all those who are “in Christ.”

Paul uses a solemn oath to persuade the Corinthians of his truthfulness. He says in effect, “If I am not telling the truth, I ask God to take my life” (Gen. 31:50; 1 Sam. 20:12; Jer. 42:5; Rom. 1:9; 9:1; Phil. 1:8; 1 Thess. 2:5).

**to spare you.** Paul would come with the Lord’s authority and power on his next visit (10:3, 4; 13:2–4, 10), and he wanted to give them a chance to repent.This was the reason he changed his plans and did not come back to Corinth before going to Macedonia. It was not worldly vacillation or cowardice, as some were saying(vv.15–17).
See Introduction: Date and Occasion.
After the painful visit (v. 1), Paul wrote a letter of rebuke (not extant) to the Corinthian church, sending it by the hand of Titus (2:13; 7:6, 7, 13, 14).

Paul’s purpose in writing the unpleasant letter was not simply to make the Corinthians sorrowful (7:8, 9). He was seeking their best interests, even when that meant bringing pain both to them and to him.
This could be a reference to the man living with his father’s wife (1 Cor. 5:1–8), but that is doubtful because the offense seems to be something directed against Paul himself (vv.5, 10).
Apparently, after Paul had left Corinth, or at least after Titus had come with the unpleasant letter, the Corinthians had exercised church discipline against the offender (cf.Matt. 18:15–20).
The purpose of church discipline is to restore, not to destroy or take revenge (10:8; cf. 1 Cor. 5:5; Matt. 18:15).

Paul will accept the judgment of the Corinthian congregation on this matter.

**in the presence of Christ.** A common theme in this epistle (2:17; 3:18; 4:2, 6; 7:12; 8:21; 12:19). All our actions are carried out not in secrecy but in the presence of Christ, the Lord of the church. If both Paul and Christ have forgiven the offender, the Corinthians should as well (cf. Matt. 16:19; John 20:23).
Satan will win a victory either if we neglect church discipline entirely, or if we attend to it but remain harsh and unforgiving when there has been a change of heart (see Luke 22:31, 32).

A city in far northwest Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), across the Aegean Sea from Greece. Having traveled north overland from Ephesus, Paul sailed from Troas to Macedonia. It was in Troas that Paul had seen a vision of a man from Macedonia imploring him to come and help (Acts 16:8).

**a door was opened for me.** God provided opportunities for preaching the gospel (1 Cor.16:9).

Paul had hoped that Titus would meet himat Troasand report that the letter of rebuke had been well received by the believers at Corinth. When Titus failed to appear, Paul was deeply troubled.

**I took leave of them.** A great opportunity for effective ministry did not make Paul turn aside from his prior commitment to care for the Corinthian church and straighten out its problems. Paul continued to feel a deep concern for all his churches (11:28, 29).

**to Macedonia.** Paul went first to Philippi, then perhaps to Thessalonica or Berea before Titus came. Acts 16:8–18:1 describes the previous journey of Paul along this route. At this point, the narrative of his relationship with the Corinthian church is interrupted until 7:5, and Paul inserts an extensive digression on the nature of the new covenant ministry in which he is engaged.

verse_quote: always leads us in triumphal procession.
note: Paul’s narrative suddenly shifts from the visible reality of his anxiety for the Corinthians and his disappointment at not finding Titus in Troas, to the spiritual realm. Paul sees himself as part of God’s triumphal procession into the heavenly city, much like a victory parade that an ancient general would lead upon returning to his own city with vanquished captives following behind the chariots. But here, Paul—God’s former enemy—is a joyful captive and one who participates in and spreads the good news of the blessings of the King’s victory. Despite setbacks like Paul’s at Troas, the eyes of faith can see the unrelenting progress of the kingdom of God.

verse_quote: we are the aroma of Christ to God.
note: That we are a sweet aroma to God means that He delights in us and in our lives. This is the more real and final fulfillment of the OT sacrifices that were a sweet aroma to God (Lev. 1:17; cf. Phil. 4:18; Eph. 5:2).

Figuratively speaking, there is apleasant fragrance, spiritually perceived, about true Christians. On the other hand, this fragrance is a “fragrance from death to death” to unbelievers, for it warns them that they are unprepared for the day of judgment (Phil. 1:28).

**sufficient for these things.** Carrying a message of eternal life or death is a sobering responsibility. No one is worthy of this solemn task, but God qualifies us for it nonetheless (3:6).

Paul may refer specifically to the “super-apostles” who propounded a “different gospel” of power and prosperity at Corinth (11:4, 5, 13–15), but the description fits the Judaizers in Galatia and elsewhere (Gal. 1:6–10) and others whose message or conduct showed them to be “enemies of the cross of Christ” (Phil. 3:18, 19). It is tragic that then and now, many preach the gospel or teach Christianity as no more than a means of earning a living (1 Tim. 6:3–5). Paul’s goal was not personal benefit or financial reward, but the glory of God.

**in the sight of God.** All Paul’s ministrywas carried out in the sight of God, providing him with a strong motive for keepinghis conscience clear (1:12;Acts 23:1; 1 Tim. 1:5;2 Tim. 1:3).See notes on 1:23 and 2:10.

Both questions in this verse expect the answer “no.” Paul does not reject letters of commendation generally (Acts 15:25, 26; 18:27; 1 Cor. 16:10, 11), but apparently Paul’s opponents had brought some misleading letters of commendation to the church at Corinth, letters of which the bearers were not worthy.

**letters of recommendation.** As church leaders or members traveled from city to city, congregations wrote letters confirming their maturity and ministry to the congregations who would receive them (Acts 18:27; cf. Rom. 16:1, 2; 3 John 5–8, 12). The “letter” confirming Paul’s ministry at Corinth, however, was far better, because it consisted of the lives of the Corinthian believers (v.2).

The Corinthians have a fixed place in his affections. Some manuscripts read “in your hearts.” On this reading, Paul is telling the Corinthians that as a church they are an effective letter of recommendation for him (2:17; 1 Cor.9:2).

verse_quote: letter from Christ delivered by us.
note:
The Corinthian church was a work of God’s grace, but in this work Paul and his co-workers had been God’s instruments (1 Cor.3:5–9).

**tablets of stone.** The Ten Commandments.

**tablets of human hearts.** Paul’s point is twofold. First, the “letter,” which the Corinthians are, is superior to the pen-and-ink letters of his opponents as well as the stone tablets of the law. Second, Paul presents the fruits of his apostleship as the fulfillment of OT prophecy. As predicted in Jer. 31:33 and Ezek. 11:19; 36:26, God promised to write His law on the hearts of His people in the new covenant, giving them a new desire and ability to obey Him. The law that is written in the heart is God’s moral law, His absolute moral standard. Paul indicates that this moral law is fulfilled in our love for God and neighbor as summarized in the Decalogue, or the Ten Commandments (Rom. 13:8–10).

After explaining his change of plans about visiting the Corinthians, Paul describes what true ministry is. It means being ministers of a glorious new covenant (3:4–4:6), trusting God in the midst of troubles (4:7–5:10), and speaking the message of reconciliation (5:11–6:13). Paul insists throughout the rest of the letter that faithfulness to these tasks—not eloquence, deep philosophical thoughts, or worldly standards of personal excellence—is the basis of avalid ministry.

**3:4 Such is the confidence.** Paul is confident before God that his ministry is authentic and that the Corinthians are “letters of recommendation” testifying to it. Paul’s confidence is not in himself, but “through Christ.”

Paul answers the question of 2:16 (“Who is sufficient for these things?”). Earlier he had disavowed any dependence on mere human ability (1 Cor. 2:1–5; cf. 2 Cor. 1:8–10). Unfortunately, Paul’s opponents valued worldly ability more than the sufficiency that comes from God alone.

**our sufficiency is from God.** A major theme of 2 Corinthians. All ability and power in ministry comes from God, not from ourselves. God deposits His treasure in human “jars of clay” (4:7), displaying His power in our weakness (12:1–10).

The new legal relationship that God established with His people through Jesus Christ, His life, death, resurrection, and ascension. The new covenant stands here in contrast to the old covenant.

**the letter.** The written laws of the Mosaic administration by themselves, which demand perfect obedience but give no power to obey (see Gal. 3:21; Rom. 8:3).

**the Spirit gives life.** This is new life in Christ. The Holy Spirit writes God’s law on our hearts (Jer. 31:31–34; Heb. 8:8–12; 9:13, 14), giving love for God’s moral standards and power to obey them (Rom.8:4; 1 Cor. 7:19). In saying that life is “not of the letter,” Paul does not imply that there was no spiritual life whatever under the old covenant. He means that the written law, which was characteristic of the old covenant, did not and could not by itself produce life in the believing community. The Holy Spirit, whose powerful, life-giving ministry is characteristic of the new covenant, does bring and alone can bring new life. Though He was active in the lives of God’s people under the old covenant, new covenant believers experience His ministry in far greater measure (Ps. 51:10–12; Joel 2:28, 29; Luke 11:13; Rom. 5:1–5).

The written words of the OT law by themselves condemned sinners, without giving them life. Elsewhere, Paul affirms that the law itself is good, but sin uses the law as a weapon to inflict death by stirring up sinful hearts to transgress the law’s good commands (Rom. 7:10–14).

**could not gaze at Moses’ face.** The old covenant was not without glory, even though it was written on stone (Ex. 34:29–35). Even so, that glory was transitory (“being brought to an end”).
The new covenant is more powerful, beautiful, and inward. Its glory is therefore greater and enduring.

Paul likely has in mind here the “righteousness” of our justification, since he contrasts it to the “condemnation” that the law of Moses pronounced on those who violated it.Righteousness is imputed to us in justification, the gracious legal declaration that begins the Christian life and that is based only on the perfect righteousness of Christ and not in any sense on anything that we do. Justification provides us with the judicial righteousness we need to stand before God unafraid (Rom. 3:21–26; 2 Cor.5:21).Having been justified, over the course of our lives we also grow in personal holiness, which remains imperfect until we are glorified and can never serve as the basis for our acceptance by the perfectly holy and righteous Creator. We can be accepted only in Christ, on account of what He has done, not what we have done (Rom. 7:14–25). This growth in personal holiness is called “sanctification,” the progressive growth of a believer in righteous thoughts, words, and deeds (Rom. 6).

verse_quote: what was being brought to an end.
note: God intended the old covenant to be replaced by a new and better covenant, as Israel’s Scriptures themselves foretold (Jer.31:31–34; Heb. 8:13).

The splendor of the new covenant, which will not fade or pass away, provides the apostle’s hope and fuels his boldness.

**very bold.** Paul is not at all ashamed to stand before the world and proclaim the excellent gospel. The reference to “boldness” links the discussion of vv. 7–11 with Paul’s defense of his apostleship (10:1, 2). He is bold, not vacillating as his opponents accused him (1:17–2:4); and his boldness, taking the form of the fearless speech so evident in this epistle, is a great contrast to the deceitful selfishness of his opponents (2:17).

Some think that Moses’s veil was to protect the Israelites from being harmed or frightened by the brightness. More likely, the veil was to keep them from seeing that the glory was fading away because of the temporary and inadequate character of the old covenant, since the narrative in Exodus shows that Moses did not put on the veil until after he had delivered to the Israelites the words God had given him on the mountain (Ex. 34:29–35). By contrast, Paul needs no veil, for the glory of the new covenant ministry does not fade away.

that same veil remains. Even today, Paul says, many Jewish people cannot see that the Mosaic covenant was temporary, and that its glory has faded.

**they read the old covenant.** Here Paul directly identifies the text of the Scriptures with the covenantal bond between the Lord and Israel, showing that God’s words are foundational to that divine-human relationship (and laying the basis for our Bibles’ division into the OT and the NT).

verse_quote: a veil lies over their hearts.
note: The metaphor shifts somewhat, as it often does in Paul’s writings. The veil is now not on Moses’s face but on his hearers’ hearts. The effect is the same—they cannot see that the old covenant fades.
Paul points to conversion as the moment at which this veil (v. 15) is lifted from the heart.

Paul stresses the close relationship between Christ and the Holy Spirit. By virtue of His resurrection and ascension, Christ and the life-giving Spirit are closely identified in function (1 Cor. 15:45). The ministry of the risen Christ, through the Spirit, under the new covenant, accounts for the surpassing glory of which Paul has been speaking.

**there is freedom.** The bondage was to death, sin, and hopeless effort to obey the law by our own power. Christ, by his Spirit, brings “freedom” from this bondage (see Gal. 5:1, 13).

All Christians. A characteristic experience of new covenant believers is described here.

**beholding.** Unlike Moses (v. 13), who alone climbed Mount Sinai to behold God’s glory as he received God’s law, we all stand “with unveiled face.” Likewise, Christians stand unashamedly before the world, reflecting in their own lives the glory of Christ beheld in the Word of God. And far from a fading glory, their glory is ever-increasing, as they are changed more and more into the likeness of Christ through the lifelong process of sanctification effected by the Spirit of God.

**into the same image.** A reference to continual growth throughout life into increasing Christlike-ness. This growth is moral and spiritual transformation “from one degree of glory to another.” Believers are being progressively restored to greater and greater possession of the image of God, which was corrupted at the fall of Adam (see Eph. 4:24; Col. 3:10).
Paul does not give up hope, despite both affliction and criticism, because the new covenant ministry in the power of the Holy Spirit is so excellent and powerful.
This means “adulterate, falsify.” Paul says he will never water down the Word of God or distort it to please his hearers (2:17). He implies that his opponents practice such deception and distortion.

The veil imagery continues from 3:14–16, now to stress that what obscures people’s perception of Paul’s message is not deception on his part but Satan’s blinding influence on the minds of those who are presently perishing (not believing in Christ).

the god of this world. Satan (cf. 1 John 5:19) strongly influences this fallen, evil world that continues until the time Christ returns and brings in fully the age to come (cf. Gal. 1:4). Satan is a deceiver who opposes the truth (John 8:44; Rev. 12:9).

**has blinded.** The result is that unbelievers cannot appreciate or fully understand the claims of the gospel unless God through the gospel inwardly enlightens them by the Holy Spirit (4:6; John 3:3; 9:39–41; Eph. 2:2, 3; 4:17–19).

**Christ, who is the image of God.** Though created in God’s image, Adam fell into sin. Christ is the image of God both as the eternal Son who reveals the Father (Col. 1:15–17) and as the sinless head of a new human race (1 Cor.15:49; Col. 3:10; Rom. 8:29).

verse_quote: what we proclaim is not ourselves.
note: The crucial issue is not whether people accept or reject Paul, but how they respond to Christ. Paul’s opponents apparently focused on themselves, and veiled Christ’s glory with their own pride.

One reason for not preaching ourselves is that only God gives new spiritual life.

**Let light shine.** God’s sovereign initiative is necessary to enable us to embrace the gospel message. Just as God’s original creative word made light where there was no light (Gen. 1:2, 3), so now God’s creative word gives spiritual life and understanding of the gospel where previously there was none.

**glory of God.** In the OT, the glory of God was the bright light that surrounded the presence of God. It led the people of Egypt as a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night (Ex. 13:21, 22). Later, it filled the tabernacle under Moses (Ex. 33:8–13; 40:34–38), and then Solomon’s temple (1 Kin. 8:10, 11). But it eventually departed from the temple in the time of Ezekiel because of the sins of the people (Ezek. 10:4, 18, 19; 11:23).It returned only in Jesus, who became flesh and dwelt among us. John says, “We have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father” (John 1:14).In contrast to the face of Moses, from which God’s glory faded (3:13), God’s glory forever shines brightly “in the face of Jesus Christ.”

The gospel ministry and the accompanying new covenant power of the Holy Spirit.

**jars of clay.** Our weak human natures, including but not limited to our physical bodies. They are a great contrast to the glory of the gospel, and Paul reminds us that God’s way is to work through those who are weak or unimpressive in the world’s eyes.

**power belongs to God.** A characteristic theme in the epistle (especially 12:1–10). Paul’s concern is always to give gloryto God, not himself.
The great evangelist and theologian also faced great discouragements.

Paul uses the key experiences of Christ (death and resurrection) as a pattern for understanding his own experiences as an apostle. Paul’s suffering and apparent defeats are evidence to all that he shares in the death of Christ (cf. 1:5). Thus, Paul can see his own sufferings as an imitation of Christ’s (1:5 and note).

**that the life.** In Paul’s weakness and sharing in Jesus’ death through suffering, Jesus’ resurrection power is continually made known (cf. Gal. 2:20; Phil. 3:10, 11).

Though Paul suffers much hardship (as Jesus did), the resultofhis ministryisspiritual lifeand resurrection power in others. This is a paradox that the world will not understand. The recipients of aministry may seem to fare much better in this world than the person who brings them the ministry, because the one who brings it may be suffering for the sake of the gospel (8:9). See 1 Cor. 4:8–13, where Paul expresses the same point with heavy irony, to humble the Corinthians’ pride.
Faith expresses itself in words that affirm confidence in what God has promised, even amid severe affliction as endured by the psalmist, whom Paul quotes here (Ps. 116:10) from the Septuagint.
God’s ultimate goal in answering prayer and bringing us the blessings of salvation is for thanksgiving and glory to be offered to Him (Is. 43:7; Eph. 1:12; Rev. 4:11).

This verse repeats the phrase from v. 1. God brings glory to Himself even through the weaknesses and discouragements of Paul’s ministry.

**our outer self is wasting away.** The contrast between outward and inward is not simply between the body and the soul, but between our whole person insofar as it still shares in the decay endemic to this present evil age and our whole person insofar as it is renewed by the resurrection power of the Holy Spirit. Yet Paul’s focus is on the body’s vulnerability to affliction in contrast to our spiritual participation in the Spirit’s vitality.

An understatement, yet Paul portrays lifelong distress as “momentary” to set it in sharp contrast to the eternity of blessing awaiting believers (see Ps. 30:5; Is. 54:7). Likewise, Paul characterizes these troubles, listed in 4:8–12; 6:4–10; and 11:23–33, as “light” (though few would consider them such) when he considers the “weight” of glory to come, to which present miseries cannot compare. These troubles are preparing a great reward for believers. Our faith and obedience in suffering pleases God, and He will not forget (Rom. 8:17, 18; 1 Pet. 1:6, 7).

**eternal weight of glory.** Troubles in this life are not only light and insignificant compared to the important and significant glory that we will enjoy for eternity, but they also “prepare” us for that glory, in the providence of God.

A frequent theme in this book (5:7, 12; 6:8–10).The unseen world is what is most real and most important; the visible world is passing away (see 1 Cor.7:31). Yet Paul is not endorsing a philosophical or religious dualism that deifies immaterial reality and devalues all things physical. He eagerly anticipates the resurrection of believers’ bodies because Christ has been raised (1 Cor. 15:12–58). He will compare the resurrection body to an eternal “house” and define Christian hope not as freedom from bodily existence (“found naked,” “unclothed”) but as being “further clothed” with glorious bodies impervious to the curse (5:1–4).

Though Paul’s and other believers’ sufferings must lead to physical death, something far greater awaits them.

**a house ... in the heavens.** This probably refers to our resurrection bodies, though some have argued that it signifies the heavenly place that God has prepared for us. Paul describes the crucified and risen Christ as the “man from heaven” (1 Cor. 15:48, 49) to show that the origin of the resurrection bodies lies in God, who through Christ has begun and will consummate anew creation.
we groan. Sighing with frustration at the limitations of this present life, with its sin, weakness, and corruption (Rom. 8:22, 23).
Without a body.

Paul longs for the resurrection body, free of the weaknesses and imperfections of this life.

**not ...unclothed.** Unlike Platonic, neo-Platonic, or Gnostic dualism, the Christian hope is not for escape from bodily existence but for the present body, a “tent” in which we “groan,” to be replaced by the resurrection body (1 Cor. 15:50–55).

**what is mortal.** Our physical bodies in their present condition and state.

**swallowed up by life.** The new, heavenly life to come will overtake our present existence. See theological note “The Last Resurrection” on p. 2040.

See note on 1:22. The Holy Spirit’s work in us now in daily renewal and spiritual strengthening (3:18; 4:16) is both the foretaste and the guarantee of future completion of that work in resurrection bodies and complete sanctification.

The believer’s perception of realityis not confined to “sight”—the present order that is seen and transient; but rather informed by “faith”—trusting in the saving promises of God that we have already begun to enjoy in Christ, but have not yet fully experienced.

The doctrine of the intermediate state between our death and Christ’s return teaches that when Christians die, they (that is, their souls) go immediately into Christ’s presence and are “at home with the Lord,” while their bodies remain here and are buried in the grave, although still united to Christ (Luke 23:43; Phil. 1:23). When Christ returns, the bodies of believers will be raised from the dead, glorified, and forever reunited with their spirits (1 Cor. 15:22, 23; 1 Thess.4:14, 16).See theological note “The Intermediate State” on p. 2109.
In whatever condition or state believers find themselves, their goal is to glorify God (1 Cor.10:31).

Degrees of reward in heaven are taught in this verse. Though Christians have their sins forgiven and will never suffer the punishments of hell (Rom. 6:23; 8:1), they will nonetheless stand before Christ at the day of judgment, to receive various degrees of reward for what they have done in this life (Matt. 6:20; Luke 19:11–27; 1 Cor. 3:12–15). This judgment will include a disclosure and evaluation of the motives of our hearts (1 Cor. 4:5).

Not a terror of eternal condemnation, but a healthy, reverent fear of Christ’s displeasure at the choices we have made, the things “done in the body” (v. 10). Such a fear would have been a healthy corrective for those Corinthians who were making trouble for Paul, and it could also have corrected the lives of many careless Christians throughout history.

**known.** Again, a spiritual viewpoint, not evident to those who judge merely by superficial appearances.

This is the world’s method of evaluation, contrary to that of a true apostle, who endures troubles by focusing on the unseen and eternal (4:18). The false apostles at Corinth (11:13) were also typical representatives of the world, taking pride in their outward appearance, relying on the self, and loving money, power, and prestige. If the Corinthians understood Paul’s self-defense in a spiritual way, they would have an answer for the false apostles and their superficial standards of judgment (1 Sam. 16:7; Is. 11:3, 4).

This probably refers to Paul’s intense zeal to glorify God in his apostolic ministry. Paul’s language does not imply complete loss of awareness of one’s surroundings, for the same Gk. word is used of people who were “amazed” at Christ’s miracles (Mark 5:42; cf. 6:51). The apostle’s point is that he lives for God and for others, not for himself (v.15). His opponents cannot make this claim.

verse_quote: the love of Christ controls us.
note:
Grammatically, this could be the love we have for Christ or the love Christ has for us. Since Paul is speaking of what Christ has done for him by dying in his place, his primary reference is to the love that comes from Christ. However, Christ’s initiating love evokes our love for Christ and others (1 John 4:7–11), and thus it “controls” our desires and relationships with others, enabling us more and more to love our brothers and sisters in Christ (Eph. 5:2; 1 John 4:7–12).

**one has died for all.** The ones for whom He died are the same as the “all” who “died” with Him as a result of His death, who are mentioned at the end of the verse (cf.Gal. 2:20). Jesus died to secure redemption and eternal life for all of His sheep, but not all people are His sheep (John 10:15, 26–28). See theological note “Definite Atonement” on p. 1875.

Paul emphasizes spiritual judgment and spiritual insight into people’s lives and situations. Our experience of Christ’s love moves us to stop evaluating others according to worldly standards and to view them instead from the standpoint of God’s great act of salvation in Jesus Christ and the divine grace that exalts the despised and humbles the proud (1 Cor.1:26–31).

**according to the flesh.** When Christ was regarded from a worldly point of view, men rejected and crucified Him as a blasphemer and troublemaker (1 Cor. 1:18; 2:8). But from the divine viewpoint, Christ is the Messiah and Son of God, in whom the new creation has come and reconciliation with God is given (1 Pet. 2:6–8).

Union with Christ summarizes our experience of redemption. Believers are elected (Eph. 1:4, 11), justified (Rom. 8:1), sanctified (1 Cor. 1:2), and glorified (3:18) “in Christ.” Here Paul focuses on the momentous significance of the believer’s union with the Savior. Because Christ is the “last Adam,” the one in whom humanity is re-created (1 Cor. 15:45; Eph. 2:10) and who inaugurates the new age of messianic blessing (Gal. 1:4; cf. Matt. 11:2–6), the believer’s spiritual union with Christ is nothing less than participation in the “new creation” (Gal. 6:15). Translating “there is a new creation” instead of the ESV’s “he is a new creation” would show more clearly that the transformation in view transcends the individual, but the thought is there either way.

The whole plan of salvation and history of redemption culminating in an end-time new creation has its origin in and is centered upon God. Paul realizes that it is from Him, through Him, and for His glory(Rom.11:36).

verse_quote: not counting their trespasses against them.
note: Objective human guilt in our violation of God’s commands has caused the alienation between sinners and their Creator. “Reconciliation” can occur only through the forgiveness of these trespasses, in which they are no longer imputed against the guilty (Rom. 4:6–8). Yet divine justice demands that sin be punished, and is satisfied by the imputation of our sin to Christ, the sinless one who bore the punishment that His people deserve on the cross (5:21).

Paul may be appealing directly to the Corinthians to “be reconciled to God,” since he later summons each member of the congregation to “examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith” (13:5). But he is also summing up the appeal he gives to all the world. Reconciliation is the establishment or restoration of loving fellowship after estrangement. For Christians, reconciliation to God is in one sense renewed each day through repentance and faith (Matt. 6:12; 1 John 1:9). All who have rested in Christ alone for salvation enjoy a reconciliation with the Lord that cannot be lost. We cannot lose the grace of reconciliation or our peace with God if we have been justified, for if we have been justified, we will certainly be glorified (Rom. 8:28–30). Nevertheless, by our sin we grieve the Holy Spirit (Eph. 4:30), and our fellowship with the Creator suffers. By our repentance, our experience of fellowship with God that is granted in our reconciliation is fully restored (1 John 1:8, 9).

An important summary of the gospel message. The verse explains how God imputed our sin to Christ. God as judge assigned the responsibility of our sin to Christ, making it possible for Him to justly receive the punishment that we deserve for that sin (Is. 53:6; 1 Pet. 2:24). The verse shows that Christ was our substitute, accepting the penalty of sin in our place. See theological note “The Sinless-ness of Christ” on p.2203.

**we might become the righteousness of God.** Not only did God impute our sin to Christ, He also imputed Christ’s perfect righteousness to us (that is, He counted it as belonging to us; Phil. 3:9). This imputation precedes the progressive realization of God’s righteousness in our moral character through sanctification. Every Christian possesses, legally, the perfect righteousness of Christ imputed by God, and received through faith alone.

If the Corinthians allow their church be swept away by the “false apostles” (11:13), or if they refuse to purify themselves from “every defilement of body and spirit” (7:1), their lives will glorify God less and less, and they may prove in the end never to have truly received God’s grace at all.

verse_quote: now is the day of salvation.
note: When God offers deliverance, it is wise to respond immedi-ately, before the offer is withdrawn. “Now” in a broad sense refers to the gospel age leading up to the return of Christ, while in a specific sense it to the time when an individual hears God’s offer of salvation. See theological note “Salvation.”

Thedistinguishing characteristics that show the authenticity of Paul’s claim to serve God are various forms of affliction, along with demonstrations of integrity, love for others, and perseverance. Implicitly, Paul is contrasting true service to the Lord with the false apostles, who shun and scorn suffering and who shade and suppress the truth for the sake of visible success.

A true minister of the gospel is known by pure speech, pure conduct, pure motives, and deep love for people.

**the Holy Spirit.** The power of the Holy Spirit was evident in Paul’s ministry, whether bringing power to his preaching, convicting unbelievers of sin (cf. John 16:8–11), or giving spiritual gifts (1 Cor. 12:7–11). This work of the Holy Spirit was another way bywhich Paul’s ministrywas commended.

Paul will not compromise the sanctity of truth or tell alie to accomplish some desirable goal (2:17; 4:2).

**the power of God.** Often to work miracles, bring healing, or silence enemies (12:12; cf. Acts 14:3, 9, 10; 19:11, 12; 20:10; 28:8, 9; Rom. 15:19).

**the weapons of righteousness.** That is, all the weaponry of God’s Spirit to be used against human or demonic opposition (10:5, 6; Acts 13:11; 16:18; Eph. 6:10–18).

A series of paradoxes again highlighting the contrast between the viewpoint of this world and the standpoint of the age to come, the standpoint invisible to the natural eye but seen by the eye of faith.
Paul reveals his inner feelings in this letter more than in any other. His “open heart” reveals his love for them.

Paul sees a deeper spiritual reality in the prohibition against unequal yoking found in Deut. 22:10.

**with unbelievers.** Note that the false apostles in Corinth claimed to be Christians but were in reality servants of Satan (11:14, 15). To join with them would distort all life and ministry in the church. The prohibition against being yoked together with unbelievers must be considered in situations where significant control over one’s actions would be willingly yielded to an unbeliever through avoluntary partnership or association. Neither Paul nor the rest of the NT tells us to have no association at all with unbelievers (Mark 2:15–17;1 Cor.5:9, 10; 7:12– 16; 1 Pet. 3:1–6). But we are told not to be “yoked together” with them in such a way that they significantly influence the direction and outcome of our moral decisions and spiritual activities.
A name for Satan.

verse_quote: we are the temple of the living God.
note:
In the OT, God’s dwelling place with His people was the tabernacle and later the temple built by Solomon. When Christ came, He was Himself the true temple or dwelling place of God (Matt. 1:23; John 2:21; Col. 2:9). Now God the Holy Spirit lives in us, and for this reason, we are the new end-time temple of God, both individually (1 Cor. 6:19) and corporately as His church (1 Cor. 3:16, 17; 1 Pet. 2:5).

**as God said.** The OT promise that God would dwell among His people (Paul’s quotation is from Lev. 26:11, 12) has become the new covenant promise that God would live in those who trust in Christ, and this has begun to be fulfilled in Christ and His people.

verse_quote: The quotation is mostly from Is.
note: 52:11 and Ezek. 20:34, though the word order is changed. This is a restoration promise about Israel’s priests, who are to leave unclean Babylon and return to build the temple. These commands to be separate now all have to do with unbelievers (cf. v. 14; note that Is. 52:11 commands Israel to go out of unbelieving Babylon). Christians are now part of the temple and also serve as priests in it; thus, they are beginning to fulfill the Isaiah prophecy by separating from the world’s uncleanness (which is reiterated in 7:1) in order to keep the temple clean. The verses do not encourage separation from believers who hold different views on certain matters, but it does involve separation from hardened false teachers (on which compare 6:14, 15 with 11:13, 15).

In this conclusion to his conflation of several OT promises of God’s presence and favor, Paul combines wording pertaining to the royal son of David (2 Sam. 7:14, 27; see Ps. 2:7) and Israel’s privilege as God’s sons and daughters (Is. 43:6; see Ex. 4:22, 23). Christians are so united to Christ that they share in His messianic sonship and the Father’s good pleasure. Separating themselves from moral impurity, therefore, is the way in which these promises call Christians to live. To give up moral defilement and to live as children of the living God is a wise and desirable choice (Phil. 2:15). Believers are to do this in realizing that they are beginning to fulfill Israel’s restoration prophecies (note the restoration background in the OT references in vv.16, 17).

The OT promises about Israel’s new temple and restoration from exile quoted in 6:16–18. These prophecies have begun to be fulfilled in Christ, the true Israel, via His return from the exile of death and restoration to the Father in His resurrection (cf. 1:20). Believers who come into union with Christ are identified with His death and resurrection and also begin, therefore, to fulfill Israel’s temple and restoration prophecies.

**let us cleanse ourselves.** Christians must take an active, vigorous role in sanctification (Phil.2:12, 13).

**every defilement.** Paul means all kinds of sin, however they come to expression in life. Physical cleanliness is not the issue, but rather conformity to God’s holy character both in one’s secret motives (spirit) and in one’s outward actions (body, or “flesh,” per text note; cf. Matt. 7:15; 1 Pet. 3:21).
Once again in defense against those who accuse him, Paul appeals to ablameless record in ministry.
Paul reveals how deeply he loves the church at Corinth; this is not deceitful speech, but an expression of his “genuine love” (6:6).

This verse resumes the narrative that broke off at 2:13. It shows Paul’s turmoil of soul when a church he deeply loved strayed from obedience to the Lord.

**Macedonia.** Northern Greece, on the way to Corinth (2:12, 13 notes).
Titus finally arrived in Macedonia with good news about the Corinthians and their response to Paul’s “severe letter.”

Paul’s “severe letter” (not extant) was written to rebuke the Corinthians for their conduct during his earlier visit (2:3, 4 notes and Introduction: Date and Occasion). The problem was probably their failure as achurch to defend Paul against the person who had wronged him. This verse shows clearly that aloving pastor must sometimes cause sorrow to those he cares for, if they fall into sin.

Turning from sin, a sincere decision to forsake aspecific sin (or sins) and to begin to obey God. Here, the term does not specifically refer to the initial repentance that always accompanies true saving faith (Mark 1:15; Acts 3:19; 17:30; 26:20) but to an ongoing turning from sin in the life of a Christian.

**leads to salvation.** “Salvation” here means not initial conversion, but growth and progress in the Christian life. Ordinary Christian growth will include times of profound sorrow for remaining sin.

**worldly grief.** Regret and sorrow of different kinds that do not seek forgiveness in Christ. The contrast between Peter’s response after denying Jesus (Matt. 26:75; John 21:15–19) and Judas’s response after betraying Him (Matt. 27:3–5) illustrates the different outcomes of godly, repentance-producing grief and worldly, death-producing grief. Jesus’ prayer for Peter made the difference (Luke 22:32).
The Corinthians responded as Paul had hoped when Titus brought the letter of rebuke.

verse_quote: the one who did the wrong.
note:
Probably not the man guilty of incest in 1 Cor. 5:1, though many have understood it this way, but a leader of opposition toward Paul himself (2:5 note).

**in the sight of God.** The Christian life is lived before the face of God. See note on 2:10.
The personal contact of the Corinthians and Titus encouraged Titus spiritually, sparking anoticeable change in him.
Apparently, even before Titus arrived with the letter of rebuke, the Holy Spirit had worked repentance in the Corinthian church.

This section concerns the collection of money for poor Christians in Jerusalem (cf. Acts 19:21, 22; Rom. 15:25–28; 1 Cor.16:1–4).

**8:1 grace.** Giving money to help other Christians in need was itself the result of God’s grace. He provided both the resources and the willingness to use them.

**churches of Macedonia.** Philippi, Thess alonica, Berea.
Paul tells the comparatively wealthy Corinthian church about the generosity of the impoverished churches in Macedonia, to the north.

They did much more than he expected.

**gave themselves.** They rededicated their lives to serving the Lord (see Rom. 12:1), and then to Paul as His servant.
Despite its troubles, Corinth was a strong church in many ways. Theyhad many spiritual gifts (1 Cor. 1:4–7;ch. 12–14), several of them listed here.
Paul wants giving to be voluntary. In general, though Paul had great authority, he preferred to ask rather than command (Philem. 14 and note), a good pattern for those in authority (Matt. 20:25, 26).

In the glory and honor that are eternally His in heaven.

**he became poor.** He gave up His heavenly glory and came to earth to live as a man and to suffer and die. The exchange described earlier as the sinless one’s “becoming” sin in order to constitute sinners righteous (5:21) is here described in afinancial metaphor—the infinitely Rich One impoverishing Himself to enrich others—in order to draw the connection to the Gentiles’ offering to relieve poverty-stricken Jewish believers. The Corinthians, like Christ, should give of themselves for the sake of others.
They had begun to give in accordance with Paul’s instructions in 1 Cor. 16:1–3.
As in all of the Christian life, so it is in giving. Good motives are not enough, but must lead to good actions in accordance with our abilities.

As the widow’s offering in Mark 12:41–44 teaches, willingness to give generously is pleasing to God, even when the gift may be small because the giver is poor.

**not according to what he does not have.** This is a warning against giving or promising to give an amount that you really do not have, hoping that God will repay it. Doing this forces a test on God (Luke 4:12). People should give as God causes them to prosper (1 Cor. 16:2). Even so, the more common offense is failing to give immediately and generously when God provides us with the resources to do so.

Not that Paul wanted all Christians to have equal possessions or equal income, but that there might be an even distribution of burdens. Paul calls for equity rather than strict equality. See Acts 4:32–35;1 Cor.11:20–22.

When the people gathered manna in the wilderness (Ex. 16:18), those who gathered more ended up with no more than those who gathered little. Now with respect to money, God’s grace in Christ must move the rich to share with those in need.
Paul is sending Titus back to Corinth ahead of him, no doubt bearing this epistle.
No name is given. Luke is a frequent suggestion.

There was some congregational role in selecting representatives to accompany Paul.

**for the glory of the Lord himself.** Giving money and administering it well is not mundane or unspiritual, but in itself honors the Lord.

Paul would not have misused any part of the gift sent to Jerusalem. He insisted that trusted representatives from several churches accompany him (Acts 20:4), in part so as to avoid even the appearance of wrongdoing. On this passage, Calvin comments that “nothing more certainly invites slanderous attacks than to be handling public money.” Moreover, the representatives would have been a sort of bodyguard for someone carrying valuables. Since these representatives came from various Gentile churches, the offering was a powerful expression of Gentile Christians’ regard for their Jewish brothers, and therefore of the church’s unity in Christ, as Paul emphasizes in Rom. 15:25–27. 8:20, 21

Not identified, though his tested trustworthiness further substantiates the fiscal reliability of the delegation that includes Titus, the brother appointed by the churches (vv. 16–19), and other brothers who represent the churches (v.23).

As the text note indicates, the Gk. term “apostles” here refers to those sent and authorized by congregations, related to those churches in a way similar to the relationship of Paul, “an apostle of Christ Jesus,” to the Lord who commissioned him with distinctive authority (1:1).
Southern Greece, where Corinth was located.

Since the Macedonians, despite their poverty, had begged for the privilege of contributing to the offering, Paul wants to avoid embarrassment both for the Corinthians and for himself, in the event that the confidence he had expressed in the latter’s generosity were to prove to be misplaced.
Paul wants to preserve the motive of willing, generous giving; the actual amount he takes to Jerusalem is of secondary importance.

An agricultural metaphor— the farmer who plants much seed reaps a large crop, but a small planting yields a small harvest. This promise is also true in the spiritual realm. Those who give generously will reap abundantly for the kingdom. What is given is never lost; it is sown. While God may at times provide a generous harvest in the physical and material realm to those who give, this is not the primary NT promise or pattern (8:9; 11:27; Luke 6:20, 21, 24, 25; James 2:5).
Giving can and should be joyful, as the Macedonians’ eagerness had shown (8:1–5).

Paul’s assurances that God “will supply and multiply your seed for sowing” and that “you will be enriched in every way” are not necessarily promises that God will reward generous contributions with financial prosperity for one’s personal enjoyment.Rather, eager givingdeepens one’s experience of God’s grace (v. 14), which sets the heart free from a grasping fixation on money and material possessions. Such “riches” enable believers to “sow” even more in generosity toward others, yielding a “harvest of your righteousness.”, 11
Through such giving, needs are met and God is thanked. The recipients’ prayers for the givers are no small reward.
Our giving is only a small imitation of God’s own excellent generosity to us, especially in the “inexpressible gift” of His Son (John 3:16).

In these four chapters, Paul deals with the problem of false apostles (11:13) who had come to Corinth and who were opposing Paul’s authority. Titus had brought good news about the previous problems at Corinth, but a new problem demanded Paul’s attention. Paul was confident in the Corinthian church (7:16), but not all the Corinthians were equally confident in Paul. Between 9:12–15 and 10:1, the tone changes abruptly from something positive to exasperation as Paul defends the genuineness of his calling as an apostle. For a discussion of this shift in tone, see Introduction: Special Issues.
A repeated theme in this epistle is living not according to worldly standards or life-views but according to spiritual power and spiritual reality.

Prayer, the proclamation of the powerful Word of God, and, for the apostles, the authority to drive away demonic opposition (Acts 16:18; Eph. 6:10–18). Also, there was a kind of powerful apostolic authority not often discussed, but apparent in the fate of Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:1–11), Saul (Acts 9:8, 9), and Elymas (Acts 13:8–12): the miraculous imposition of judgment, foreshadowing the ultimate expression of God’s wrath at the end of history.

**strongholds.** Paul may refer to spiritual strongholds, that is, centers of demonic opposition to the gospel (1 Pet. 5:8, 9; 1 John 5:19). Paul knew his opponents at Corinth were servants of Satan (11:14, 15), but that did not frighten him, for the power of the Holy Spirit within him was far greater. On the other hand, Paul identifies the “strongholds” destroyed by the spiritual weapons he wields with “arguments” and “every lofty opinion” that resists God, and he speaks of taking “every thought captive” (v.5).So Paul’s military imagerymay describe the effects of the gospel whenever the Holy Spirit breaks through the defenses of a fallen human heart to seize and subdue it to Christ.

False wisdom and sophisticated arguments were some of the weapons used by the servants of Satan in their attack against Paul. The apostle had earlier stressed the difference between the wisdom of the world and the spiritual wisdom of the cross, and he warned the Corinthians against being deluded by the wisdom of the world (1 Cor. 1:18–2:16). Now Paul sees that his opponents have made such inroads with their false wisdom that he must oppose it again in the strongest terms and, at the same time, regain the loyalty and obedience of the Corinthians.

**every thought captive.** If every thought, then the whole person—every idea, motive, desire, and decision—belongs to Christ.

If the Corinthians join ranks in opposing the false apostles, Paul is ready to punish these opponents for the harm they do. This may be the imposition of church discipline by his unique apostolic authority, although Paul does not specify the form that the punishment might take.
Paul knows that he must now call upon the authority Christ has given him and warn the Corinthians that he is readyto use it (v.4 note).

Paul did not depend on the kind of trained oratory prized by the world and designed to get glory for the speaker (1 Cor. 2:3–5). Those influenced by the opponents attacked Paul’s ministry by saying he lacked this skill.
See notes on vv.4, 6.

Now the matter surfaces that caused Paul to defend his apostleship so vigorously. Encouraged by rival “apostles,” some influential Corinthians had begun to compare these latecomers to Paul—with Paul coming out the loser. He was judged deficient as a speaker (v. 10; 11:5), weak in his relationship with the church (vacillating between boldness while absent and timidity when present; vv. 10, 11), unloving toward them (in refusing a monetary gift that, in their view, snubbed them as inferiors; 11:7–11; 12:14– 18), and deficient in certain religious experiences of “power” (12:1–5 and notes). But Paul refuses to compare himself to his opponents on their shabby terms of self-boasting and self-promotion. When he yields and boasts to them (11:16–18), he does so ironically, using the form of comparison but always refusing their false values.

Paul will take credit only for things that God has permitted him to do, but this includes having come to Corinth as their apostle. He implies that the opponents in Corinth with their boasting were intruding into his area of responsibility (v.14).
Paul was hoping the Corinthians would prosper spiritually and become a base from which he could go on and evangelize beyond them, presumably to Rome and then to Spain (Acts 19:21; Rom. 15:22–29).

9:24, a text that Paul quoted in his earlier epistle to humble the Corinthians’ pride and party spirit (1 Cor. 1:31). To “boast” in something means to declare how great something is. All of Paul’s boasting in this letter ultimately ends up givinggloryto God.

The Lord’s judgment is final, and will set aside every human judgment. Paul has been careful not to make any claim except what is based on God’s purposes and on what God has done. He concludes the section with the very basic principle that a person should look for the approval of God and not man, and especially not one’s own self-commendation (Matt. 6:1–4; John 5:44; Rom. 2:29; 1 Cor. 4:3, 4; Gal. 1:10).

Paul longs for the Corinthians to remain loyal to Christ. He uses a metaphor of engagement and marriage. If the Corinthians follow the false apostles, they will stray from Christ and be unfaithful to Him. Then they can no longer come to Him as a “pure virgin.” It is assumed that God’s ideal for marriage is no prior sexual relations—that a bride would come as a “pure virgin” to her husband, as her husband would also come to her. Paul evokes the rich OT and NT imagery of the Lord’s marriage to His people as His bride (Jer. 2:1, 2;Ezek. 16; Hos.1–3; John 3:29, 30; Eph. 5:25–27; Rev. 19:6–8; 21:2, 9–26).
Paul knows that the false apostles are a dangerous spiritual threat, comparable to the serpent in Eden (vv.14, 15; Gal. 3:1).

verse_quote: another Jesus ... different spirit ... different gospel.
note: The strongholds, arguments, and pretensions (10:4, 5) of Paul’s opponents so distort the truth that their so-called “Jesus,” “spirit,” and “gospel” differ radically from what Paul has preached (1 Cor.1:18–2:16; cf.Gal. 1:6–9). The “different gospel” of the opponents conforms to worldly ways of thinking so much that Paul and his apostolic ministry—a ministry manifesting the death of Jesus through adversity and suffering (4:7–18; 6:4–10; cf. 1 Cor. 4:8–13)—is despised and rejected in favor of ministries that satisfythe current taste for eloquence, philosophical wisdom, and spectacular displays of spiritual power (cf.1 Cor.1:22–25).

There is a hint of mockery in Paul’s use of this inflated title for his opponents in Corinth. It may even be a name they applied to themselves. Some think that they used it to refer to the Jerusalem apostles. Yet, although some may have compared Paul unfavorably to the original apostles, honoring them as “pillars” (Gal. 2:9), Paul himself regarded Peter, John, and the rest of the Twelve as partners in the gospel, not competitors (Gal. 2:7–10). The “super-apostles” in Corinth, on the other hand, were in fact “false apostles” (v.13).
See note on 10:10.

When Paul was at Corinth he supported himself (Acts 18:3) and accepted help from other churches as well (v. 8). Some of the Corinthians seem to have been offended by Paul’s refusal to accept their gift, probably offered to him in response to his preaching of the gospel to them. In ancient times, giving and receiving gifts was often used to establish and maintain friendships among social equals, as well as to signal dependents’ subordination to patrons. In this system, Paul’s refusal of a gift might be taken as an insult, a proud refusal to be involved with inferiors. But the apostle views his relationship with the Corinthians, not from the standpoint of worldly social convention (5:16), but from the standpoint of the new creation (5:17) in which he has been called to be an apostle and spiritual father. As a father, he may rightly give to his children without receiving anything in return (12:14, 15). Moreover, as Paul previously explained to the Corinthians, he considered it aprivilege to “present the gospel free of charge” (1 Cor. 9:19) so that, when he first came to a new city, the mode of his communication illustrated the grace of his message.
Probably from Philippi (Phil. 4:15, 16; Acts 18:5 note).

Paul had ministered to the Corinthians at great personal sacrifice and expense—unlike the false apostles, who apparently were demanding support from the church (cf. vv.7, 20).

**the regions of Achaia.** The area around Corinth.
Paul’s opponents at Corinth were not just fellow Christians who differ in certain nonessential matters; they were actual servants of Satan inside the church, competing for its leadership.

One of Satan’s tricks is to claim to be doing good, and specificallyto send to achurch servants of his who purport to be Christians, but who bring only division, slander, immorality, and all kinds of destruction. Jesus told His disciples, “You will recognize them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:20; cf. Acts 20:29, 30; 2 Pet. 2).
Final judgment by God.
A description of some of the bold actions of the false apostles, which seem to have included exploiting others financially and demanding unbefitting obedience and honor.

This part of the letter is known as the “Fool’s Speech.” In it, Paul describes his ministry in terms that could not possibly be equaled by the false apostles. Yet he does not boast about his own knowledge or speaking skills or other abilities, but about how much he has suffered for the sake of Christ. Here Paul’s boasting is ironic—he “boasts” of things normally considered shameful, signs of weakness and defeat. Thus, his boasts are an imitation or parody of the boasting of his opponents, who praised themselves to the Corinthians in extravagant speeches. The topics in this section progress to a climax where Paul deals with what may have been uppermost in the minds of his critics—unusual religious experiences (12:1–9).

**11:22 Are they Hebrews.** Paul’s opponents were Jews, perhaps coming from Jerusalem and claiming to be endorsed by the Jerusalem apostles. Paul can match at every point the false apostles’ claims with respect to Israelite heritage (Phil. 3:4, 5).

In recounting the marks of a true servant of Christ, Paul points not to displays of power (though he could; 12:12) but rather to suffering and humiliation, emphasizing again Christ crucified (as he did in 1 Cor.1–4).

**11:23** Paul reveals his extreme hesitancy to speak at all on his own behalf.
According to Deut. 25:3, forty lashes was the maximum that could be inflicted on a person. It was Jewish practice to set the limit a little lower as a safeguard against miscounting.

One such occasion is reported in Acts 16:22.

**Once I was stoned.** In Lystra on Paul’s first missionary journey (Acts 14:19), where the crowd thought they had killed Paul.

**Three times I was shipwrecked.** A shipwreck is recorded in Acts 27:39–44, but 2 Corinthians was written earlier, at the time described in Acts 20:2 (when Paul was in Macedonia). The three shipwrecks must have happened during his earlier missionary journeys.

Paul’s goal was not his own personal comfort or safety. Many of the hardships he records in this larger section are not recorded at all in Acts. It is hard to imagine a more hazardous existence than Paul had, yet he was obedient to God and put his life in God’s hands.

**false brothers.** People pretending to be Christians, who came into the Corinthian church to stir up trouble.
Paul felt deeply the needs and suffering of his churches. His trust in God’s sovereign care did not make him cold or unemotional.

This incident is narrated from a different standpoint in Acts 9:24, 25. Apparently, Paul’s Jewish opponents in Damascus persuaded the governor to cooperate in their plot against Paul. Although these two verses may seem somewhat surprising in the context, they mention Paul’s first—and rather humiliating—experience of being persecuted (rather than persecuting others) for the sake of the gospel. The apostle makes a precarious escape from arelativelyminor civil authority, like a common fugitive. He is not presenting himself as ahero., 33

In these verses, Paul continues his “boasting” with the topic of a vision of heaven. His account contains some unexpected elements. Paul is not permitted to repeat the things he heard in the vision, and afterward he receives apainful “thorn” (v. 7 note) sent by God to keep him humble.

Although he speaks indirectly and even seems to distinguish between the recipient of the vision and himself (v. 5), Paul clearly means himself, as becomes clear in v. 7. Through this transparent pretense of distancing himself from an anonymous individual so privileged to receive a visionary revelation, Paul’s example signals his strong disapproval of self-promotion (10:18).

**third heaven.** According to a common enumeration, the first heaven is the atmosphere of the birds and clouds, the second is the sky in which we see the stars, and the third is heaven, the invisible dwelling place of God. For fourteen years, Paul had not made this experience a focus of his teaching, as some would have done. His focus was the message of Christ: “What we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord” (4:5).

That is, the “third heaven” of v. 2. The Gk. word for “paradise” (derived from a term meaning “garden”) is used with various meanings outside the NT, but in the NT, all three occurrences (v. 3; also Luke 23:43; Rev. 2:7) refer to heaven, the place where the saints dwell with God.
Paul wanted people to evaluate him on the basis of their firsthand knowledge of him.

Many possibilities have been suggested for this “thorn,” such as a physical ailment of some sort (“in the flesh”; cf. Gal. 4:13–15), a harassing demon (“a messenger of Satan”), or the constant harassment of Jewish persecutors. Throughout the history of the church, no agreement has been reached among hundreds of commentators. As it stands, the “thorn” of Paul’s experiences is readily applied to a variety of trials faced in this life. Few of God’s servants have been free from at least some kind of hindrance, weakness, or opposition.

Paul’s usual expression to refer to Christ, not to God the Father. Although prayers in the NT are most often directed to God the Father, this is an example of prayer directed to Christ (cf. Acts 1:24; 7:59; 1 Cor. 16:22; Rev. 22:20). It is striking that in his “boasting,” Paul testifies about a request that God did not fulfill.

verse_quote: my power is made perfect in weakness.
note: God will accomplish His purposes without taking from His servant the thorn that seems to hinder him. Despite human weaknesses, God’s grace accomplishes His purposes in a fallen world. This promise from God no doubt gave Paul strength and encouragement in subsequent sufferings. Paul shortly ties the general principle to its source—the cross of Christ (13:4). Paul’s whole response to attacks on his apostolic authority has been patterned consciously on Christ and Him crucified, and not on the so-called “Jesus” and the different “gospel” that his opponents foisted upon the erring Corinthians (11:4 note).
Paul’s spiritual view is so clear that he can see his sufferings as reasons for rejoicing, for he knows that in them all of Christ’s power is at work.

Paul has to “boast” about his apostolic weakness because the Corinthians, who know him well, have not defended him against the false apostles, but instead have been seduced (11:1–3) by inflated self-claims and untrue criticism of Paul.

Paul identifies the “signs of a true apostle” with miracles, “wonders and mighty works.” Throughout this epistle, Paul also points to other marks that distinguish him from the false apostles: the changed lives of the Corinthians (3:2, 3), the blameless character of his ministry (6:3–10; 7:2; 8:20, 21), his genuine love for his churches (6:11, 12; 7:3; 11:7–11), and his sacrificial endurance of suffering (6:3–10; 11:23–33). In addition to these marks, Paul is ready to mention miraculous signs as divinely authenticating his apostolic ministry. See 1 Cor. 13:2; theological note “The Apostles” on p. 1912.

See Introduction: Date and Occasion. The first visit was on Paul’s second missionary journey (Acts 18:1–18). The second visit (2:1) is not recorded in Acts but occurred sometime during Paul’s extended stay at Ephesus (Acts 19:1–41).

**I seek not what is yours but you.** Unlike those preachers whose goal is their own financial reward.

verse_quote: got the better of you by deceit.
note: Perhaps Paul’s opponents were saying that his apparent selflessness was a trick to deceive them. Paul answers that he never exploited them through others (v. 17).
Titus was coming ahead of Paul (8:6, 16, 17).

Paul again emphasizes that he has not been speaking for his own reputation or glory but for the good of the church and for the glory of God. Again he reveals a strong awareness that everything he writes and does is “in the sight of God.” See note on 2:10.

Paul’s fatherly ties with the Corinthian church are strong, and he knows that if he returns to find some of them (his “children,” v. 14) still unruly, it will be humiliating for him, just as parents are humiliated by the misbehavior of their children.

**many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented.** False apostles were not the only problem in Corinth. There were some people still engaging in sin, and Paul warns them (see 1 Cor. 5:1, 2; 6:9–20).

See note on 12:14. Paul quotes Deut. 17:6 and 19:15. The “two or three witnesses” likely does not mean Paul’s two or three visits to Corinth (for Paul is still only one witness), but is rather a reminder that when he comes, all charges will be considered fairly and dealt with in a just way. On the other hand, in view of his apostolic authority from Christ, he may be implying that each of the warnings he previously delivered both in person and by letter constitutes a distinct testimony or evidence to establish a “case” against those who resist God’s truth.
A strong statement of Paul’s apostolic authority. Christ Himself was speaking through Paul, and Christ’s words through Paul would powerfully silence any offenders.

Paul’s life (as that of all Christians) was united with Christ in His death and resurrection, and he continued to share in the resurrection power of Christ as long as he lived (see 4:10–12; Phil. 3:10, 11).

See 1 Cor. 11:28; Gal. 6:4. Paul’s words help clarify the doctrine of assurance of faith. Paul asks the Corinthians to examine their own lives for evidence of salvation. Such evidence would include trust in Christ (Heb. 3:6), obedience to God (Matt. 7:21), growth in holiness (Heb. 12:14; 1 John 3:3), the fruit of the Spirit (Gal. 5:22, 23), love for other Christians (1 John 3:14), positive influence on others (Matt. 5:16), adhering to the apostolic teaching (1 John 4:2), and the testimony of the Holy Spirit within them (Rom. 8:15, 16).
Christians in the church from which Paul was writing (see Introduction: Date and Occasion).

A Trinitarian benediction, corresponding to the threefold placing of the Lord’s name upon Israel in the benediction pronounced by OT priests (Num. 6:23–27). See theological note “The Triunity of God” on p. 1204.
